goal: Intuition Lab is an autonomous visual physics research lab with humans in the loop. Its goal is to build intuitive understanding of physics through honest, interactive, beautiful visuals, publishing one reviewed investigation a day, and over time to work toward clearly scoped investigations of open problems in physics. Agents propose, research, render, review and revise; the owner steers through picks, questions, feedback and approvals. Scientific honesty, beginner clarity and low cost matter more than volume.

proposals.title: Require every percentage readout to name what it is a percentage of
proposals.problem: Ambiguous comparative percentages recur across topics. twin-trip's 'Traveller comes home younger by 56.4%' reads as '56.4% younger in total age'; attention's "'animal' falls to about 30%" was corrected to 'about a third' for accuracy; light-clock's frozen counters imply a 0.33 ratio that disagrees with the authoritative 0.436 labels. Readers cannot tell the referent of a bare percentage.
proposals.proposal: Add a validation rule that any scene-data readout or body sentence containing a percent value must also carry an explicit referent phrase (e.g. 'of the home twin's aged time', 'of the attention total'). Implement as a check that a percent token is accompanied by a nearby 'of ...' or an allowed referent pattern, and surface the offending string for rewrite. Pair it with a one-paragraph phrasing rule in the brief/curriculum guidance so authors write 'ages 56.4% less during the trip' rather than 'younger by 56.4%'.
proposals.benefit: Removes a whole class of misreadable numbers before render, directly addressing three separate reviewed/needs_review guides with one rule.
proposals.risk: Pattern matching on 'of' may be noisy and could nag correctly-phrased lines; keep it a warning the reviewer clears, and tune patterns against the known good examples.

proposals.title: A picture for “If gravity slows time, why do things fall?”
proposals.problem: No visual engine can show this question yet, so the daily run cannot investigate it.
proposals.proposal: Things fall because standing still means racing through time, and when clocks tick slower lower down, the straightest path through time quietly tips downward. Falling is that tilt: you keep going straight, but "straight" now leans toward the slow clocks. Chapter 1: A person stands still on the ground. A clock floats at their head and another at their feet; both tick. A faint readout compares the two rates. Chapter 2: The scene flips to a spacetime map: vertical axis is time, horizontal axis is space. The still person becomes a single arrow pointing almost straight up. Chapter 3: The time axis
proposals.benefit: The daily run could then investigate “If gravity slows time, why do things fall?”.
proposals.risk: Needs hand-built drawing code, model checks and a beginner test before it is marked ready.

proposals.title: A picture for “Can two events be simultaneous for one person but not another?”
proposals.problem: No visual engine can show this question yet, so the daily run cannot investigate it.
proposals.proposal: "At the same time" is not a fact everyone shares. Whether two events count as simultaneous depends on how you are moving. There is no single universal "now" stamped on the universe. Chapter 1: Side view of a train car. A lamp dot sits dead center; the rear (left) and front (right) walls are equidistant, each carrying a small stopped clock. The rider stands beside the lamp. Chapter 2: Same car in the rider's frame. Two light pulses leave the lamp as equal expanding arcs heading to each wall. Chapter 3: The same flash, but now the whole car glides rightward past a still platform observer below.
proposals.benefit: The daily run could then investigate “Can two events be simultaneous for one person but not another?”.
proposals.risk: Needs hand-built drawing code, model checks and a beginner test before it is marked ready.

proposals.title: Mobile length caps on why and beat titles
proposals.problem: Copy overflows the mobile layout: light-clock's why is 33 words against the roughly 25-word target, and twin-trip's chapter title is too long for one mobile line. Both returned as review findings that a cheap automated check would have caught first.
proposals.proposal: Add a validation check that the one-line why is at most about 25 words and each beat title fits one line at the mobile breakpoint, measured by rendered width against the known title style with a conservative character fallback. Emit a warning with the current length and the limit. Apply the caps only to why and titles, not to subtitle bodies, because other findings require adding words (for example defining 'light-year') and bodies must stay free to do that.
proposals.benefit: Near-zero-cost fix for two recurring findings; frees reviewer attention for substance.
proposals.risk: A rigid character cap can force awkward truncation, so measure against the actual mobile title style where possible and treat the cap as a reviewer-overridable warning, not a hard block.

proposals.title: Predict-first beat built from standard wrong answers
proposals.problem: Investigations explain the right answer but don't ask the beginner to commit to a guess first. Without that, an existing misconception may never come to the surface. 'Common wrong answers' are currently written by the model, with nothing to anchor them.
proposals.proposal: Add an optional prediction field to the scene schema: one question and two or three choices, exactly one of them correct. Show it as a tap-to-answer card before the reveal chapter. The renderer reveals the result and then names which wrong intuition each wrong choice reflects. Where a PhysPort concept test covers the topic, for example force and motion for falling-time, the reviewer must check that the wrong choices match documented misconceptions and record the citation. Without such a source, the card is labelled 'author's guess'. No answers are stored on the site, so it stays static.
proposals.benefit: Predicting before seeing an answer, with implicit scaffolding, is a well-established way to build intuition, and it fits PhET's design approach. Sourcing the wrong answers keeps the misconception claims honest.
proposals.risk: PhysPort pages were not opened today, so check coverage and licensing before relying on it. Concept inventories cover mechanics well but quantum and relativity topics less well. A poorly written question can plant a new misconception.

proposals.title: Respect reduced motion and add a real pause control
proposals.problem: The hero stage runs looping canvas animations with timed subtitles. WCAG 2.2 SC 2.2.2 (Level A) requires a pause, stop or hide control for motion lasting more than 5 seconds. The renderers may also ignore the user's reduced-motion setting.
proposals.proposal: Give the hero stage and the card previews a single shared playback controller. It provides a visible pause/play button, also on the spacebar, which pauses subtitles too, and arrow-key chapter stepping. It reads matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)'), and when that is set it shows each chapter's key frame instead of the loop and autoplays nothing, including card previews. Add one headless capture with reduced motion emulated to the existing render check.
proposals.benefit: Meets a Level A requirement, helps beginners who need time to read, and lets learners hold a frame while they move the sliders. Doing it in one controller keeps the engines simple.
proposals.risk: Engines need a deterministic 'key frame' for each chapter, so a few may need small changes. The WCAG and MDN details are recalled from memory and should be checked.
